posts.title: Fixed or variable: a calm look at home loans
posts.excerpt: Three questions to ask before you choose, with one worked example.
posts.content:
Rates have moved twice this year, and our clients ask the same thing: should we fix? We start with three questions instead. How much could your monthly payment rise before it hurts? How long do you plan to stay? And how much do you keep in savings?

For a household with a large cushion and a short horizon, variable often still makes sense. For a young family on one income, the certainty of a fixed rate can be worth paying for. Bring your loan papers to a single-question meeting and we will run both numbers with you.

posts.title: How big should an emergency fund be?
posts.excerpt: Not a rule of thumb, but a number built from your own fixed costs.
posts.content:
You will often read “three to six months of salary”. We prefer to start from fixed costs: rent or loan, insurance, school fees and food. Add them up for one month, then ask how long it would take you to replace your income if it stopped.

Keep that amount in an ordinary savings account, separate from your everyday one, and do not invest it. Once it is full, everything else you save can go to work for the long term.

posts.title: A pension for freelancers, one invoice at a time
posts.excerpt: Why a fixed percentage works better than a yearly lump sum.
posts.content:
Freelancers tell us the same story: they meant to put money into a pension in December, then the tax bill arrived. The fix is simple. Every time an invoice is paid, move a fixed share of it to three places: tax, a buffer and the pension.

Ten per cent to the pension is a good start. In a slow month the amount is small, in a good month it is large, and nobody has to remember anything in December. We check the numbers with you each quarter.
